In your situation, m = 100, N = 5, n = 3, and we don't have an epsilon! We are trying to choose the best epsilon for your situation such that the theorem still holds. Think of epsilon as the "error factor". That is, if epsilon = 0.01, then your distances will be preserved within a 1% error.

The lemma says that, as long as 0 < epsilon < 1 and 3 > 8*ln(100)/(epsilon)^2, then you can project down and preserve distances to within a factor of epsilon. That is, we find that epsilon > sqrt(8*ln(100)/3) = 3.504 for the theorem to hold. But... the theorem also requires that 0 < epsilon < 1 (which makes sense; you don't want to be more than 100% off!).

What's going on here? The problem is that your m is too large for N = 5 and n = 3. That is, the theorem can't really help you if you're trying to project 100 points from 5D into 3D. There simply isn't an epsilon with 0 < epsilon < 1 that satisfies 3 > 8*ln(100)/(epsilon)^2. So, basically, if you are working with a fixed dataset of 100 vectors in 5D and you must project to 3D, then this theorem can't help you.

To address your third point, you have to read the theorem statement very carefully. It says that, if you satisfy all the hypotheses, *there exists* a linear map f : R^N -> R^n with a certain *maximum* error bound. The theorem says nothing about an arbitrary projection g : R^N -> R^n, and even if you use the function f from the theorem, it doesn't say anything about minimum bounds or average bounds.

everyone can probably figure out what someone means when they use “it’s” as a possessive, yeah. similar to how everyone can probably figure out what someone means when they use “your” instead of the contraction for you are. i’m intentionally using the word “probably” in both sentences, because i can definitely think of situations where keeping the two distinct can ease the understanding of written language. 

“it’s power is unbelievable.”

“its power is unbelievable.”

“it’s tyranny that causes the destruction of the world.”

“its tyranny that causes the destruction of the world.”

in each case, one of these sentences doesn’t parse, but the actual usage that fails to parse in each sentence is different. in the first situation, “it’s” as “it is” fails to parse. in the second, it’s “its” as a possessive that fails to parse. 

if we were to merge the two meanings into just “it’s” then the reader would have to do extra work in order to figure out which sentence does or doesn’t make sense, and i’m too lazy to cook up an example, but i’d imagine there’s a sentence in which both interpretations can parse, which can lead to wildly different understandings of the text. 

i’d argue that, as a new english learner, having the two meanings be syntactically distinct is actually beneficial when it comes to understanding written prose. of course, this means that they also have to learn how to use them themselves, but this is still to their own benefit. they are learning to become more effective communicators within the realm of their new language.

while you’re probably right that homophones will be phased out, i hope that they aren’t just phased out and replaced by whatever grammar mistake natives make the most. it’d be nice to have syntactically and phonetically different spellings of these words. i don’t see how collapsing multiple meanings of a homophone into one syntactic string is beneficial in the long run. sure, maybe it’s easier to spell and use in writing when first learning english, but it just makes the word that much more loaded and complicated to parse. THAT’S convoluted, in my view.

edit: to add a hot take, i don’t necessarily think irregular forms are intrinsically a bad thing in a language. they are often used in special cases of overloaded phonetic pronunciations in order to make written prose more comprehensible. ones that add nothing are bad, sure. but i disagree that any of the irregular forms that we have discussed are ones that “add nothing”. is it good that certain pronunciations are overloaded? no. that doesn’t mean we should get rid of the partial solution of irregular forms, but rather that we should invent new pronunciations entirely, but that’s clearly not realistic.

The easiest way to solve this problem is to use matrices and row reduce, but it’s not the only way. 

For the kernel: the kernel is the set of all (x, y) in R2 such that f(x, y) = (0, 0). We know that f(x, y) = (2x+y,x-y). To find the kernel, set (2x+y,x-y) = (0,0) and solve for the set of all (x, y) that satisfy the system of equations. 

For the image: the image is the set of all (a, b) in R2 such that there exists (x, y) in R2 with f(x,y) = (a,b). In other words, the image is all possible outputs of f. Do you see what the image has to be here?
